question: A person removed revenue stamps from documents on June 28, 2024, but was not discovered until July 10, 2024. The stamps were reused on July 5, 2024. Which law governs the removal and the reuse?
assistant_reply:
The removal on June 28, 2024 is governed by the Indian Penal Code because it occurred before July 1, 2024. The reuse on July 5, 2024 constitutes a separate act of using Government stamp known to have been before used under BNS Section 184, because it occurred after the BNS came into force. The removal and reuse are distinct acts with different dates. The BNS applies to the reuse even though the removal was pre-BNS. The prosecution must charge the removal under the IPC and the reuse under BNS Section 184. The temporal jurisdiction depends on the date of each specific act.

Legal Analysis (IRAC):
Issue: Which law applies when removal is pre-July 1 but reuse is post-July 1?
Rule: The BNS applies to acts committed on or after July 1, 2024. Removal and reuse are separate acts.
Application: The removal is a completed offense under the IPC on June 28. The reuse on July 5 is a new offense under BNS Section 184. The date of the reuse determines the applicable law for that specific act. The pre-BNS removal does not immunize the post-BNS reuse.
Conclusion: The removal is charged under the IPC and the reuse under BNS Section 184.

Core legal principle: Removal before July 1, 2024 is governed by the IPC, while reuse after July 1, 2024 is governed by BNS Section 184.

question: A person erased usage marks from stamps on June 29, 2024, and sold the stamps on July 2, 2024. Which law applies to the erasure and the sale?
assistant_reply:
The erasure on June 29, 2024 is governed by the Indian Penal Code because it occurred before July 1, 2024. The sale on July 2, 2024 is governed by BNS Section 185 because it occurred after the BNS came into force. The erasure and sale are distinct acts. Even though the sale is of the same stamps altered before July 1, the act of selling occurs after the transition and is governed by the BNS. The BNS Section 185 explicitly covers selling or disposing of stamps from which marks have been erased, regardless of when the erasure occurred. Therefore, the sale charge falls under BNS Section 185 while the erasure charge falls under the IPC.

Legal Analysis (IRAC):
Issue: Which law applies when erasure is pre-July 1 but sale is post-July 1?
Rule: The BNS applies to acts committed on or after July 1, 2024. Erasure and sale are separate acts.
Application: The erasure is a completed offense under the IPC. The subsequent sale is a new act under BNS Section 185. The BNS provision explicitly criminalizes selling stamps from which marks have been erased, making the sale itself the punishable act regardless of when the erasure occurred.
Conclusion: The erasure is charged under the IPC and the sale under BNS Section 185.

Core legal principle: The sale of stamps with erased marks after July 1, 2024 is governed by BNS Section 185, while the erasure before that date is governed by the IPC.

question: A forged will was created on June 20, 2024 and used to claim property on September 5, 2024. Does the IPC or BNS govern this offense, and what is the legal test for determining temporal applicability?
assistant_reply:
The BNS governs this offense. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 came into force on July 1, 2024. Since the forged will was created on June 20, 2024 (before July 1, 2024), technically the IPC Section 467 would apply to the act of creation. However, the continuous offense doctrine may apply if the forgery was used on September 5, 2024. More precisely, under the general principles of temporal jurisdiction, the law in force at the time of the offense governs. Since the creation (the substantive offense) occurred June 20, 2024, IPC 467 applies to the forgery creation. However, the use on September 5, 2024 would be governed by BNS Section 340 (using forged document as genuine) as a separate offense. The Supreme Court has held that when an offense is continuing or has multiple components, the law at the time of each component applies. The CBI passport scam case (SC_0024) illustrates how courts analyze document forgery cases with multiple temporal elements.

Legal Analysis (IRAC):
Issue: Does IPC or BNS govern a forgery created before July 1, 2024 but used after?
Rule: Law in force at offense commission governs; separate acts may have separate governing laws; BNS effective July 1, 2024.
Application: Creation on June 20, 2024 governed by IPC 467; use on September 5, 2024 as separate offense governed by BNS 340; continuing offense doctrine may apply to link temporal components.
Conclusion: IPC 467 governs creation; BNS 340 governs post-July use; court must analyze whether single transaction or separate offenses.

Core legal principle: The law in force at the time of offense commission governs; for continuing offenses or separate acts (creation vs. use), different laws may apply to different temporal components.

question: On June 25, 2024, an Indian citizen committed an act of extortion in Nepal. The BNS came into force on July 1, 2024, replacing the IPC 1860. Can the accused be prosecuted under the BNS, and what is the specific transitional provision governing this scenario?
assistant_reply:
The accused cannot be prosecuted under the BNS for an offence committed on June 25, 2024. Section 358(2)(c) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 explicitly provides that the repeal of the Indian Penal Code shall not affect any penalty or punishment incurred in respect of offences committed against the Code so repealed. Since the act was committed when the IPC was still in force, the prosecution must proceed under IPC Section 384 (the IPC equivalent of extortion). Section 358(3) clarifies that anything done or any action taken under the IPC shall be deemed to have been done or taken under the corresponding provisions of the Sanhita, but this applies to actions taken after the commencement of the BNS, not to the substantive offence itself which was committed prior to the transition date.

Legal Analysis (IRAC):
Issue: Whether the BNS applies retroactively to offences committed before its commencement on July 1, 2024.
Rule: Section 358(2)(c) preserves penalties and punishments for offences committed against the IPC prior to its repeal. Section 358(1) repeals the IPC with effect from July 1, 2024.
Application: The general principle under Section 6 of the General Clauses Act 1897, which is preserved by Section 358(4), provides that the repeal of an enactment does not affect any liability incurred under the repealed law unless the new enactment expressly provides otherwise. The offence of extortion was completed on June 25, 2024, creating a liability under the IPC. The BNS does not expressly provide for retroactive application to completed offences. Therefore, the liability remains under the IPC framework despite the subsequent repeal.
Conclusion: The prosecution must proceed under IPC Section 384, not under the BNS, because the offence was committed before the BNS came into force.

Core legal principle: Section 358(2) saves penalties for offences committed under the IPC prior to the BNS commencement date of July 1, 2024.

question: A person commits the offense of using a previously used Government stamp on June 15, 2024. Which law applies and why? What would be the legal consequence if the same act were committed on July 15, 2024?
assistant_reply:
For the June 15, 2024 act, IPC 1860 Section 262 applies because the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 came into force on July 1, 2024. The IPC continues to govern offenses committed before this date. If the same act were committed on July 15, 2024, BNS 2023 Section 184 would apply as the substantive equivalent. The temporal jurisdiction is determined by the date of commission, not the date of trial or investigation. This transition is governed by the repeal and savings provisions in BNS 2023 Section 358 and BNSS 2023 Section 531, which ensure continuity of proceedings and preserve liabilities for pre-commencement acts under the IPC while applying BNS to post-commencement acts.

Legal Analysis (IRAC):
Issue: Which substantive law governs a stamp offense committed on June 15, 2024 versus July 15, 2024?
Rule: BNS 2023 effective July 1, 2024. Pre-July 1, 2024 acts governed by IPC; post-July 1, 2024 acts by BNS. BNS 358 and BNSS 531 contain repeal and savings provisions.
Application: June 15, 2024 falls before commencement: IPC 262 applies. July 15, 2024 falls after commencement: BNS 184 applies. The date of offense commission controls, not subsequent proceedings.
Conclusion: IPC 262 for June 15, 2024; BNS 184 for July 15, 2024.

Core legal principle: The BNS 2023 came into force on July 1, 2024; pre-commencement acts are governed by IPC, post-commencement by BNS.

question: A riot occurs on June 20, 2024 involving force used by an unlawful assembly. Does IPC or BNS apply, and how does the temporal jurisdiction analysis differ if the assembly formed before July 1, 2024 but the force was used after?
assistant_reply:
IPC 146 (rioting) applies to the June 20, 2024 act as it occurred before BNS commencement on July 1, 2024. However, if the assembly formed before July 1 but the force constituting rioting occurred after July 1, BNS 191 would apply to the post-commencement acts. The key analytical distinction is that rioting (BNS 191/IPC 146) is a distinct offense from unlawful assembly (BNS 189/IPC 141)â€”the 'rioting' is completed upon use of force in prosecution of common object. Under BNSS 518 (continuing offense), if the force was used continuously across the commencement date, the post-July 1 acts would be governed by BNS 191. The temporal analysis requires identifying: (1) when the unlawful assembly formed; (2) when force was first used; (3) whether force was continuous or discrete acts; and (4) whether any discrete act of force occurred after July 1, 2024.

Legal Analysis (IRAC):
Issue: Which law applies to rioting when assembly formed before but force used across BNS commencement?
Rule: Rioting completed upon force use. BNS applies July 1, 2024. BNSS 518: continuing offenses deemed committed each day. Discrete acts vs. continuous force affect temporal determination.
Application: June 20, 2024 force: IPC 146. If assembly formed June 20, force continued past July 1: post-July 1 force acts governed by BNS 191 per BNSS 518. Must analyze discrete vs. continuous force application.
Conclusion: Complex temporal analysis: date of force use governs; continuing force may trigger split jurisdiction with BNS for post-commencement acts.

Core legal principle: Rioting is a distinct completed offense upon use of force; temporal jurisdiction depends on when force was used, with continuing force potentially triggering BNS for post-commencement acts under BNSS 518.

question: If a gang rape occurred on June 15, 2024, which law would apply and what would be the procedural and evidentiary differences compared to an offense committed after July 1, 2024?
assistant_reply:
For an offense on June 15, 2024, the Indian Penal Code 1860 would apply, specifically IPC Section 376D (gang rape). The procedural framework would be the Code of Criminal Procedure 1973 (CrPC), not BNSS 2023. The evidentiary law would be the Indian Evidence Act 1872, not BSA 2023. Under CrPC, there was no explicit mandatory in-camera trial provision for rape (though later amendments introduced some protections). Under the Evidence Act 1872, there was no statutory presumption of absence of consent equivalent to BSA Section 120; the general rule was that the prosecution had to prove absence of consent. The victim's character could potentially be more scrutinized. After July 1, 2024, BNS Section 70, BNSS Sections 184 and 52 (mandatory medical examinations), BSA Section 120 (presumption of non-consent), and BSA Section 48 (irrelevance of victim's character/sexual history) apply, creating stronger procedural and evidentiary protections for victims.

Legal Analysis (IRAC):
Issue: Which law applies to gang rape committed before July 1, 2024 and how does it differ from post-July 1, 2024?
Rule: Pre-July 1, 2024: IPC 376D, CrPC 1973, Evidence Act 1872. Post-July 1, 2024: BNS 70, BNSS 2023, BSA 2023 with enhanced victim protections.
Application: June 15, 2024 offense falls under IPC regime without mandatory medical exams, without statutory consent presumption, with potentially admissible character evidence. Post-July 1 offenses have mandatory BNSS 184/52 exams, BSA 120 presumption, BSA 48 character exclusion.
Conclusion: IPC applies to June 2024 offense with weaker victim protections; BNS/BNSS/BSA apply post-July 2024 with stronger procedural and evidentiary safeguards.

Core legal principle: The temporal cutoff of July 1, 2024 determines whether IPC/CrPC/Evidence Act 1872 apply or BNS/BNSS/BSA 2023 apply, with significant differences in victim protections and evidentiary presumptions.

question: If the sale occurred on June 25, 2024, and the accused was arrested on July 5, 2024, which substantive and procedural laws apply, and how does the BNS savings clause operate?
assistant_reply:
IPC 1860 Section 258 applies substantively because the sale occurred on June 25, 2024, before BNS commencement. However, the arrest and subsequent proceedings on July 5, 2024, fall under BNSS 2023 and BSA 2023. Under BNS Section 358, for pre-commencement offenses, investigations and trials shall continue as if BNS had not been passed, meaning IPC 258 governs the offense definition and punishment. Under BNSS Section 5, the BNSS applies to all proceedings including those for pre-commencement offenses, so arrest, bail, investigation, and trial procedure follow BNSS 2023. Under BSA Section 1, the BSA applies to all proceedings, governing evidence and proof. The equivalent BNS provision (Section 257) would apply only if the act occurred on or after July 1, 2024.

Legal Analysis (IRAC):
Issue: Which laws apply when sale occurred June 25, 2024 but arrest was July 5, 2024?
Rule: Offense date determines substantive law: June 25, 2024 = IPC 258. BNS 358 saves IPC for pre-commencement acts. BNSS 5 and BSA 1 apply procedural laws to all proceedings regardless of offense date.
Application: Sale date controls: IPC 258 substantive. Arrest and proceedings after July 1, 2024 follow BNSS 2023 (arrest under Sections 35-48, investigation under 173-193) and BSA 2023 (evidence rules).
Conclusion: IPC 258 substantive; BNSS 2023 and BSA 2023 procedural.

Core legal principle: IPC applies substantively to pre-commencement acts; BNSS and BSA apply procedurally to all post-commencement proceedings; BNS 358 preserves IPC for pre-commencement offenses.

question: Compare the elements of IPC Section 153 and BNS Section 192. If provocation was given on June 28, 2024, but the riot occurred on July 3, 2024, which law governs the provocation and which governs the riot, given Section 358(3) of the BNS?
assistant_reply:
IPC Section 153 and BNS Section 192 are substantially similar in their core elements, both punishing wanton provocation with intent to cause riot. For the provocation given on June 28, 2024, IPC Section 153 would govern because the act of giving provocation occurred before the BNS came into force on July 1, 2024. For the riot that occurred on July 3, 2024, BNS Section 191 would govern the rioting itself because the substantive offense of rioting was completed after the transition date. Section 358(3) of the BNS provides that anything done or any action taken under the IPC shall be deemed to have been done or taken under the corresponding provisions of the BNS. This deeming provision ensures procedural continuity, but the substantive liability for the provocation remains governed by the IPC because the act was committed before July 1, 2024. The charge sheet would properly cite IPC Section 153 for the provocation and BNS Section 191 for the riot, with Section 358 ensuring that the proceedings are not defective due to the transition.

Legal Analysis (IRAC):
Issue: Whether the riot occurring after July 1, 2024, can be deemed a consequence of the pre-transition provocation for purposes of liability under Section 192.
Rule: Section 192 requires that the riot be committed in consequence of the provocation, with the provocation being the actus reus and the riot the consequence.
Application: A complex jurisdictional issue arises when the cause (provocation) is under the IPC and the effect (riot) is under the BNS. The liability for the provocation itself is determined by IPC Section 153, while the liability for participating in the riot is determined by BNS Section 191. The causal link between the two is a question of fact, not law, and does not affect which statute governs each respective act.
Conclusion: The provocation is governed by IPC Section 153 and the riot by BNS Section 191, with the causal connection between them being a factual matter for the trial court.

Core legal principle: Acts committed before July 1, 2024, are governed by the IPC, while acts committed after are governed by the BNS, with Section 358(3) ensuring procedural validity of cross-transition proceedings.

question: If the assembly formed on June 25, 2024 and the murder was committed on July 5, 2024, which code governs the substantive offense and why?
assistant_reply:
This presents a complex temporal jurisdiction issue. The assembly formation (June 25, 2024) occurred before BNS 2023 commencement (July 1, 2024), but the substantive offense (murder on July 5, 2024) occurred after. Under criminal law principles, the governing law is determined by the date of the substantive offense (actus reus), not the preparatory acts. However, the assembly's formation under IPC 141 might be considered for evidentiary purposes regarding common object existence. The BNSS 2023 would apply for all procedural aspects. This follows the principle that penal statutes apply to offenses committed after their commencement, regardless of preparatory acts before commencement.

Legal Analysis (IRAC):
Issue: Which code applies when assembly formed before but offense committed after BNS commencement?
Rule: Penal statutes apply to offenses committed after commencement. Actus reus date controls, not preparatory acts. BNS 1: commencement July 1, 2024.
Application: Assembly formation June 25, 2024 is preparatory. Murder July 5, 2024 is substantive offense. BNS 190 (IPC 149 equivalent) and BNS 101 (murder) apply. IPC 149 does not govern despite pre-formation.
Conclusion: BNS 2023 governs substantive offense; assembly formation date relevant only for common object evidence, not code applicability.

Core legal principle: Substantive offense date (July 5, 2024) determines applicable code, not preparatory assembly formation date (June 25, 2024); BNS 2023 applies to post-July 1, 2024 offenses.

question: An order was promulgated by a public servant on 29 June 2024. The accused knew of the order on 30 June 2024 but disobeyed it on 2 July 2024. Which law applies to the disobedience, and what is the corresponding IPC provision?

The corresponding IPC provision was Section 188 (Disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant). The crucial date is the date of the offence (disobedience), not the date of the order's promulgation or the date of knowledge.

Legal Analysis (IRAC):
Issue: Which law applies when an order was issued before the BNS commencement date but disobeyed after?

The corresponding IPC provision was Section 188, which has been replaced by BNS Section 223.
Conclusion: The BNS Section 223 applies because the disobedience occurred after 1 July 2024, regardless of the order's earlier promulgation.

Core legal principle: The law in force at the time of the commission of the offence governs, regardless of when the order was issued or when knowledge was acquired.

question: A search under BNSS 97 is conducted on July 15, 2024 for forged documents related to an offense committed on March 20, 2024. The search reveals both physical forged property documents and digital smart contracts. Which substantive law governs the forgery offenses, and how does this affect the evidentiary framework?
assistant_reply:
The substantive law governing the March 20, 2024 forgery offenses is IPC 1860: IPC 463-465 (forgery and punishment), IPC 466-467 (forgery of records/valuable security), and potentially IPC 468 (forgery for cheating). This is because the offenses predate July 1, 2024 BNS commencement. However, the BNSS 2023 procedure including Section 97 search applies per BNSS Section 4(1) 'and other laws' clause. The evidentiary framework becomes hybrid: (1) For physical forged documents: BSA 56-60 (documentary evidence), BSA 65-71 (proof of execution), BSA 72 (comparison of signatures); (2) For digital smart contracts: BSA 61 (electronic record definition), BSA 63 (admissibility with certificate), BSA 62 (special provisions), BSA 90 (presumption as to electronic messages), BSA 85-87 (presumptions as to electronic agreements/signatures/certificates); (3) The BNS 2023 definitions in Sections 335-336 (false document, forgery) do not apply substantively but may inform interpretation; (4) Trial procedures under BNSS 530 (electronic mode) apply regardless of substantive law vintage. The savings clause BNSS Section 5 ensures procedural applicability to pre-commencement offenses.

Legal Analysis (IRAC):
Issue: Which law governs March 2024 forgery offenses found in July 2024 BNSS 97 search, and what evidentiary framework applies?
Rule: IPC 1860 Sections 463-468 govern substantive offenses (pre-July 2024). BNSS 97/530 apply procedurally per Section 4(1) 'other laws'. BSA provides dual framework: 56-72 (physical), 61-63/85-90 (digital).
Application: March 20, 2024 offenses: IPC 463-468. July 15, 2024 search: BNSS 97 valid. Physical documents: BSA 56-72. Smart contracts: BSA 61-63/85-90. Trial: BNSS 530 electronic mode. No ex post facto violation as procedural law.
Conclusion: IPC substantive, BNSS procedural, dual BSA evidentiary framework for hybrid physical-digital evidence.

Core legal principle: BNSS 97 search for pre-July 2024 forgery applies IPC 1860 substantive law with BNSS 2023 procedure, creating hybrid evidentiary framework: BSA 56-72 for physical documents, BSA 61-63/85-90 for digital evidence, with BNSS 530 electronic trial.

question: If an abetment occurred on June 15, 2024 under IPC Section 107, and the principal offence was committed on July 5, 2024, how would Section 46 of the BNS apply to determine the abettor's liability for the person abetted's incapacity?
assistant_reply:
The abettor would be liable under BNS Section 46 because the act abetted was committed after July 1, 2024. Under Section 358(3) of the BNS, the abetment commenced under the IPC is deemed to be under the BNS. Section 46 of the BNS, like its predecessor IPC Section 108, provides that the abettor is liable even if the person abetted is incapable by law. The provision maintains the principle that abettor liability is independent of the principal offender's capacity, ensuring continuity from IPC Section 108 to BNS Section 46.

Legal Analysis (IRAC):
Issue: Determining applicable law when abetment spans the IPC-BNS transition date.
Rule: Section 358(3) deems IPC acts to be under BNS, and the BNS applies to acts committed after July 1, 2024.
Application: Since the substantive offence occurred after commencement, BNS Section 46 applies. The substantive rule regarding incapacity remains consistent with IPC Section 108.
Conclusion: The abettor is liable under BNS Section 46 for the offence committed after July 1, 2024.

Core legal principle: Abettor liability for an incapable person abetted continues from IPC Section 108 to BNS Section 46, with the BNS applying to acts committed after its commencement.

question: A robbery occurred on June 20, 2024 at a bank. The accused was arrested on July 5, 2024. Does IPC Section 390 or BNS Section 309 apply, and what is the significance of the offense date versus arrest date?

The arrest date (July 5, 2024) is irrelevant for substantive law applicability; it only affects procedural matters under BNSS which applies to all pending proceedings. Legal Analysis (IRAC):

Rule: BNS Section 1: commencement July 1, 2024. Substantive law determined by offense date, not arrest date.
Application: Offense date June 20, 2024 precedes BNS commencement. Therefore IPC 390 governs substantive offense. BNSS governs post-July 1, 2024 procedural aspects of investigation and trial.
Conclusion: IPC 390 applies to substantive offense; BNSS applies to procedures after its commencement; arrest date is irrelevant for substantive law.

Core legal principle: Substantive criminal law applies based on offense commission date; BNS applies prospectively from July 1, 2024; arrest and procedural dates do not affect substantive law applicability.
